title: LG-Bench: A Graph-Structured Evaluation Benchmark for Life Sciences
topic: Data-centric AI->Data-centric AI methods and tools
claim: Flat, list-based benchmarks treat related questions independently and miss inconsistencies; a graph structure links them and exposes the failures.
layout: 3 panels: two question cases on top, arrow down to comparison banner
description: A case study on a pale yellow background. The top row has two dashed-outline panels. Each shows a cartoon scholar asking a speech-bubble multiple-choice biomedical question about 9p21/CDKN2A loss in EAC. The left LLM answer is wrong (red X, correct answer D). The right LLM answer is correct (green check). The two questions are semantically related, and the key term EAC is highlighted in red in both. A large gray arrow points down to a bottom banner. On the left, a robot asks "Why can I only answer one of two similar questions correctly?" Below it, a yellow scribbled box labeled "Traditional Benchmark" lists "List-based, Independent evaluation, Structure-lacked, Isolated questions" next to a stack of Q1–Q5 tags, with Q2 and Q4 in red. On the right, "LG-Bench" has blue-underlined keywords (semantic connections, topological reasoning, graph-based, structured) beside a small node-link graph. Its nodes are blue for correct answers and red for incorrect ones, with a legend.
caption: Case study comparing LG-Bench with traditional benchmarks. Unlike traditional list-based approaches that overlook semantic connections, LG-Bench utilizes a graph structure to capture these links, effectively revealing LLM inconsistencies on related questions.
abstract: Traditional evaluation benchmarks reduce inherently interconnected scientific knowledge in life sciences into flat lists of questions, disregarding the underlying topological structure of the knowledge. We introduce LG-Bench, the first graph-structured benchmark for life sciences, featuring over 10,000 high-quality multiple-choice questions across medicine, biology, and chemistry. Our approach constructs a weighted evaluation graph using bidirectional matching and semantic similarity algorithms, where nodes represent questions and edge weights capture their semantic relationships. Leveraging this graph topology, we design two novel evaluation metrics. The Global Coherence Score (GCS) measures a model's consistency within semantically related neighborhoods, while Knowledge Balance Score (KBS) analyzes how model errors are distributed across the graph to reveal conceptual blind spots. LG-Bench facilitates fine-grained comparison of LLMs by surfacing differences in conceptual coherence and patterns of knowledge organization across models. Our framework shifts the evaluation paradigm from flat accuracy metrics to structure-aware analysis, offering a new lens for diagnosing and improving LLM performance in the life sciences domain.
